topic.title: FERC Rejects PJM's AI Curtailment Plan: Does the Grid Bottleneck Just Move to the States?
topic.trigger: On October 9, 2026, FERC issued its order in Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (cited by secondary sources as 197 FERC Para 61,019, with Commissioner Rosner's concurrence) on PJM's companion Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) / Large Load Registry / BYONC filing: it accepted PJM's 50 MW Large Load definition and Large Load Registry (effective October 12, 2026) but rejected the IRAS curtailment-priority framework and bring-your-own-new-capacity (BYONC) provisions as encroaching on states' retail-rate jurisdiction. This is the exact open watchlist event from this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report and directly engages an explicit 'invalidate' kill condition set on the August 28, 2026 PJM/BYONC thesis.

questions.primary: Does FERC's October 9, 2026 rejection of PJM's IRAS/BYONC curtailment-priority framework (Docket ER26-3515) invalidate this pipeline's August 28, 2026 finding that PJM's capacity-rationing policy reveals a structural firm-generation bottleneck, or does it simply relocate the rationing mechanism from a single federal framework to a fragmented, state-by-state patchwork while the underlying scarcity persists?
sub: What exactly did FERC accept versus reject in its October 9, 2026 order, and on what legal/jurisdictional grounds?

Does this order satisfy the explicit 'invalidate' kill condition set in the August 28, 2026 report's thesis, and what does that mean for the thesis as a whole versus just its policy-mechanism component?
What does PJM's own public reaction and industry/law-firm commentary reveal about where curtailment-priority authority is likely to land next?
Does the rejection change the underlying dispute over who pays an estimated $29.4 billion in data-center-driven PJM capacity costs?
How does this order interact with the separate, still-pending Reliability Backstop Procurement hearing (ER26-3380) covered in this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report?

thesis: FERC's October 9, 2026 order granted PJM's Large Load definition and registry but rejected the Interim Resource Adequacy Service curtailment-priority and BYONC provisions as intruding on states' retail-rate authority -- squarely meeting the August 28, 2026 thesis's own 'invalidate' kill condition for that specific federal policy mechanism. But the order does not resolve, and arguably sharpens, the underlying structural bottleneck: PJM's firm-generation shortfall (reaffirmed independently by this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report as a third-consecutive-year Base Residual Auction shortfall) is untouched by this ruling, while authority over who gets curtailed first and who pays an estimated $29.4 billion in data-center-driven capacity costs now shifts to a fragmented patchwork of individual state proceedings -- with Pennsylvania and Ohio flagged by analysts as likely first movers -- rather than a single federal framework. The practical effect looks less like resolving a bottleneck and more like trading one (an unresolved federal rulemaking) for another (a potentially inconsistent, slower-moving set of state-by-state regimes).

facts.statement: On October 9, 2026, FERC issued an order in Docket No. ER26-3515-000 that accepted PJM's proposed 'Large Load' definition (50 MW or more of demand at a single site) and PJM's Large Load Registry, effective October 12, 2026, while rejecting the companion Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) curtailment-priority framework and the Bring-Your-Own-New-Capacity (BYONC) provisions.

Multiple secondary reports describe FERC's stated legal reasoning as jurisdictional: the IRAS curtailment obligations fell directly on new large loads that are largely retail customers, and the proposed compensation framework for IRAS appeared to function as a retail rate -- a matter FERC held belongs to the states under the Federal Power Act, not to PJM or FERC.

FERC rejected the BYONC provisions and related capacity-market (VRR curve) changes alongside IRAS because it viewed them as inextricably linked to the rejected curtailment framework, rather than severable and independently approvable.

One source's docket appendix cites the order as 'Order Accepting Tariff Revisions in Part and Rejecting Tariff Revisions in Part,' PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, 197 FERC Para 61,019, issued with a concurrence from Commissioner Rosner.

Commissioner Rosner's concurrence argued that curtailment-priority rules for large loads are properly a state responsibility, that PJM should stand ready to adjust its own operations, and that curtailment should be used only after voluntary demand response has been exhausted.

A PJM spokesperson said the company is reviewing the order to determine how to meet FERC's requirements while recognizing the responsibilities the Commission indicated belong to the states, described the accepted registry and definition as 'a step in that direction,' and declined to elaborate on PJM's next steps while the review is underway.

Several outlets reported the outcome was largely anticipated by market participants and that load-serving aggregators were not particularly worried about the ruling, because most stakeholders already expected individual states -- rather than PJM or FERC -- to adopt their own IRAS-style curtailment or large-load regimes, with the new PJM Large Load Registry providing states the underlying data to do so.

Industry commentary following the order named Pennsylvania and Ohio as the states most likely to lead in adopting their own curtailment-priority or bring-your-own-power-style rules for large loads, following each state's prior executive or regulatory actions on data centers.

PJM's own Independent Market Monitor, Joseph Bowring, stated that data-center-driven capacity charges totaled $29.4 billion across PJM's last four Base Residual Auctions -- 46% of the $63.6 billion in total capacity charges over that period -- with data centers accounting for $6.3 billion of $16.4 billion (about 38%) in the most recent auction alone.

FERC's October 9, 2026 order did not itself allocate or quantify the $29.4 billion in data-center-driven capacity costs the Independent Market Monitor had identified; the broader 'who pays' question remained explicitly unresolved after the ruling.

PJM's IRAS/Large Load Registry/BYONC filing in Docket ER26-3515 was the same companion filing this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report identified as still undecided past PJM's requested October 12, 2026 effective date, and as separately protested by PJM's own Independent Market Monitor and by the Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA).

inferences.statement: Because FERC rejected the curtailment-priority and BYONC provisions specifically on jurisdictional grounds -- not on a finding that curtailment priority is unnecessary or that the underlying capacity shortfall is overstated -- the ruling most directly kills the particular federal policy vehicle this pipeline's August 28, 2026 report examined, while leaving open (and effectively inviting) a state-by-state or PJM-refiled successor mechanism to take its place.

Because this order addresses only the curtailment-priority/BYONC policy layer and leaves PJM's firm-generation shortfall -- independently reaffirmed by this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report as a third-consecutive-year Base Residual Auction shortfall -- completely untouched, the underlying Structural Bottleneck classification for firm dispatchable generation in PJM should not be revised based on this order alone.

Because multiple states (at minimum Pennsylvania and Ohio, per industry commentary) are expected to pursue their own curtailment-priority or large-load rules using the data now generated by PJM's FERC-approved Large Load Registry, the practical result of this ruling looks less like eliminating a rationing mechanism than fragmenting it into a potentially slower, less consistent set of up to 13 separate state-level processes across PJM's footprint.

Because market reaction to the order was described as muted and largely anticipated, rather than triggering fresh alarm, financial markets appear to be pricing this as a procedural redirection of an already-expected policy fight rather than as new evidence the AI-data-center power bottleneck is easing or worsening.

unknowns: Whether and when PJM will refile a FERC-compliant successor to the IRAS curtailment framework, and whether such a refiling would restore most of the original mechanism or something materially narrower, is unknown.

Whether Pennsylvania, Ohio, or other PJM-member states will actually adopt binding curtailment-priority or BYONC-style rules -- as opposed to non-binding guidance or no action -- and on what timeline, is unknown.
The precise eventual allocation of the $29.4 billion in data-center-driven capacity costs identified by PJM's Independent Market Monitor was not determined by this order and remains unresolved.
The full text and legal reasoning of FERC's October 9, 2026 order, including whether any commissioner dissented rather than concurred, could not be independently verified from the sources available.

All primary FERC, PJM, and company-investor-relations domains attempted (ferc.gov, elibrary.ferc.gov, pjm.com, insidelines.pjm.com, en.wikipedia.org and others) returned DNS/connection failures under the research environment's egress policy; facts rely on convergent search-result snippets describing the order and secondary/law-firm summaries rather than direct verification of the order's full original text.

bottlenecks.node: Firm dispatchable generation capacity in PJM
bottlenecks.expansion_time: 3+ years (gas turbines), longer where financing/siting lags
bottlenecks.rationale: FERC's October 9, 2026 order addressed only curtailment-priority policy, not generation supply; the third-consecutive-year Base Residual Auction shortfall this pipeline's October 1, 2026 report documented is wholly unaffected by this ruling, so the underlying physical scarcity remains a reaffirmed Structural Bottleneck.

bottlenecks.node: Federal (FERC-level) curtailment-priority rulemaking for new large loads
bottlenecks.rationale: This specific channel is now closed at the federal level: FERC rejected the IRAS/BYONC curtailment framework on jurisdictional grounds. As an administrative rationing mechanism rather than a priced market, it is honestly Neutral, and its near-term relevance as a near-term national pathway has fallen further since the August 28, 2026 report.

FERC's order explicitly directs this authority to the states, and PJM's newly approved Large Load Registry supplies the data for states to act; multiple states can move at different paces and with different rules, so this qualifies as a growing but non-monopolized, substitutable venue rather than a strict bottleneck.

bottlenecks.node: BYONC-contracted dedicated generation for large loads
bottlenecks.rationale: With the federal mandatory BYONC mechanism rejected, voluntary dedicated-generation contracting (as Vistra's Comanche Peak-Amazon deal demonstrated, per this pipeline's September 6, 2026 report) remains available to well-capitalized developers as a workaround, consistent with a Growth Area rather than a Structural Bottleneck.

bear_case.argument: FERC's rejection was narrowly jurisdictional (retail-rate authority), not a finding that curtailment priority is unneeded; PJM can refile a redesigned IRAS compliant with FERC's guidance, potentially restoring a federal framework relatively quickly.

The underlying firm-capacity shortfall is unchanged by this ruling -- neither better nor worse -- so this order is a procedural/jurisdictional event, not new evidence that physical scarcity is intensifying.

Multiple outlets described the outcome as largely anticipated and said aggregators were 'not particularly worried,' suggesting markets had already priced in this specific rejection rather than being newly destabilized by it.

Large, well-capitalized developers can still pursue BYONC-style dedicated generation contracts voluntarily (as Vistra's Comanche Peak-Amazon deal showed) even without a FERC-mandated curtailment framework, limiting the practical effect on the best-funded players.

This order does not itself quantify or allocate the $29.4 billion cost question; the 'who pays' dispute remains open and could resolve in a way that is either favorable or unfavorable to large-load developers, independent of this specific ruling.

kill_conditions.metric: FERC action on any PJM refiling in Docket ER26-3515 or a successor docket
kill_conditions.threshold: FERC approval of a revised curtailment-priority framework within 2 quarters of a PJM refiling

kill_conditions.condition: Fewer than two PJM-member states adopt any comparable curtailment-priority or large-load rules within 12 months, leaving large loads largely unconstrained
kill_conditions.metric: Count of PJM-member states adopting state-level large-load/curtailment rules
kill_conditions.threshold: Fewer than 2 of 13 PJM-member states adopt comparable rules within 12 months

kill_conditions.condition: PJM's capacity shortfall closes in a subsequent Base Residual Auction, reducing the practical stakes of any curtailment-priority mechanism
kill_conditions.metric: PJM BRA cleared capacity vs. reliability requirement
kill_conditions.threshold: A subsequent auction clears at or above the 20% reliability target with no shortfall
